newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Africa investment climate improving-Coca Cola.
newsitem.headline: Africa investment climate improving-Coca Cola.

text.p: Carl Ware, Coca Cola senior vice-president and president of the company's Africa Group, said late on Wednesday that political and economic reforms in Africa were attractive to foreign investors and that Coca Cola expected to double its business in Africa in the next five years.

"We believe very strongly that Africa as a whole is setting forth the necessary preconditions for investment, that is economic and political reform and in particular getting the issues of foreign exchange control, issues of investment incentives for private industry, tax reform sorted out," he said.

He told Reuters at the Africa African-American summit being held in Harare to drum up U.S. investment for the continent that the consumer market in Africa was also getting younger, more urban and more educated and it had also developed a skills base to manage businesses, all preconditions for investing there.
"We are finding that all of those necessary conditions are available in Africa and therefore we are very very aggressive in our investment strategy in Africa," Ware said.
He said as one of the world's emerging markets, Africa contributed less than 10 percent of total Coca Cola global sales pointing to scope for growth.

"Our goal is to double our business in the next five years in Africa. That means that we will grow at double digit growth rate every year compounded to reach one billion unit cases (per year) within the next five years," he said.
Currently, the corporation sells 600 million cases per year in Africa.
Ware said Coca Cola would "soon" be opening bottling plants on the island states of Cape Verde and Mayote and was talking to the Angolan government about investment prospects there.

The corporation announced in February various investments for some sub-Saharan African countries, including $275 million it and its seven bottlers said it was investing in South Africa to strengthen its market share there and $60 million it said it would invest in Zimbabwe over the next four years.
"We are committed to Africa...We are not trying Africa to see if it works. This is the real thing. We are investing in Africa not retreating," Ware said.
